strengths: High Practical Relevance: The paper directly addresses the critical memory and runtime bottlenecks of state-of-the-art optical flow models (like RAFT and its derivatives) when processing ultra-high-resolution (UHR) images, enabling native 4K and 8K flow estimation on standard hardware.

Mathematically Exact Drop-In Replacement: The proposed block-sparse correlation sampler computes the exact same operator as RAFT's full correlation volume. This allows it to be used as a drop-in replacement with existing pre-trained models without any retraining or loss of accuracy.
Substantial Performance Gains: The method achieves up to 95% lower memory usage compared to the default dense precomputation, and is up to 90% faster than the standard on-demand sampling method.

New UHR Evaluation Benchmark: The authors generate and introduce a high-quality 8K ground-truth optical flow dataset based on the Blender movie 'Charge', providing a valuable new benchmark for high-resolution optical flow evaluation.

Thorough Evaluation and Analysis: The paper contains extensive experiments across multiple hardware platforms (RTX 3090, 4090, A100, GH200), detailed component breakdowns, complexity derivations, and thorough qualitative/quantitative analyses.
weaknesses: Limited Novelty of Cascaded Inference: The test-time cascaded inference (coarse-to-fine flow initialization) is a relatively straightforward pyramid-like heuristic. While it successfully mitigates large-displacement issues at high resolutions, its algorithmic novelty is minor.

Overhead at Low Resolutions: Due to the bookkeeping overhead (mask generation, block-sparse indexing, and caching), the proposed method can be slightly slower than the default dense matrix multiplication at very low resolutions (e.g., standard Sintel/KITTI resolutions), though this is negligible in absolute time.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical bottleneck in modern optical flow estimation: the quadratic computational and memory complexity of the all-pairs correlation volume at ultra-high-resolutions (such as 4K and 8K).

The proposed block-sparse sampling algorithm is mathematically exact, meaning it maintains identical accuracy to the original RAFT operator while achieving a sub-quadratic memory complexity of O(P^{1.5}).
The engineering of the solution is very solid, introducing a patch-major data layout to increase sparsity and a caching mechanism across iterations to avoid redundant computation.

The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning isolated operator tests, multiple hardware platforms (RTX 3090/4090, A100, GH200), traditional benchmarks, and a newly rendered 8K ground-truth optical flow dataset based on the Blender movie 'CHARGE'.
The proposed cascaded inference strategy allows SEA-RAFT to handle large displacements at high resolutions without requiring any retraining, achieving state-of-the-art results on 8K flow estimation.
weaknesses: At lower resolutions (e.g., standard Sintel/KITTI scale of ~512x1024), the management overhead of constructing the computation mask and updating the cache limits the runtime speedups compared to the default dense implementation.

The core of the speedup relies heavily on custom CUDA kernels (as noted in Section 8.2). While pseudocode is provided, the paper would benefit from a more detailed discussion in the main text regarding the exact threading layout and memory access patterns that make this implementation efficient on modern GPU architectures.
A direct comparison against other sparse attention or localized cost volume baselines (beyond the RAFT-style variants) would have further contextualized the efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and important bottleneck in optical flow: the quadratic memory and computational complexity of RAFT's dense 4D correlation volume when processing ultra-high-resolution (UHR) 4K/8K images.
The proposed block-sparse correlation volume sampling algorithm is mathematically exact compared to RAFT's default operator, ensuring no accuracy degradation while achieving up to 95% memory savings.

The authors introduce a new high-quality 8K optical flow evaluation dataset rendered from the Blender movie 'Charge', complete with ground-truth flows, providing a valuable benchmark for high-resolution correspondence tasks.
Comprehensive hardware and runtime analysis across multiple GPUs (RTX 3090, RTX 4090, A100, GH200) demonstrates solid speedups over standard on-demand sampling at high resolutions.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed 'cascaded inference' test-time extension is a straightforward coarse-to-fine initialization heuristic that is well-known in both classical and deep optical flow literature.

The system-level optimizations (such as masking, caching, and block indexing) introduce considerable overhead, making the approach yield negligible or zero runtime improvements at standard lower resolutions (e.g., Sintel, KITTI, and Spring as shown in Tables 8-10).

The paper reads more like a GPU systems/engineering optimization paper rather than a computer vision methodology paper, as the core contribution is an efficient CUDA implementation of an existing operator rather than a new formulation of optical flow.

The selection of block size B is critical for balancing sparsity and hardware utilization (as analyzed in Section 8.1), but the paper lacks a systematic or automated way to select this parameter dynamically for different input scales and GPU architectures.
